web_title: 1. Origin, Corporate Evolution & Past Stock Cycles
book_title: Chapter 1: How the Business & Stock Got Here — Past Cycles & Pivots
title: A Survivor That Keeps Building Into Headwinds
question: What has this company already lived through, and does its record show a business that compounds through cycles or one that overbuilds into them?

epigraph.quote: “It was to be expected that interest and depreciation burdens will exert significant pressure on the bottom line.”
epigraph.author: Xpro India Directors’ Report, Annual Report FY2014-15, on the first dielectric film line [11]

web_blocks.html: Xpro India was incorporated on 26 November 1997 as Biax Films Limited. It had a first subscription of seven shares of ₹10, and a fresh certificate dated 22 September 1998 gave it its present name [12]. The operating units came from another company. The Placement Document records share allotments on 4 February and 30 June 2000 under a scheme of arrangement between Cimmco Birla Limited and Xpro India. The High Courts of Calcutta and Madhya Pradesh sanctioned the scheme by orders dated 12 April and 7 October 1999 [12]. The company itself says that, through a corporate demerger in 1998, it was established as a separate entity. The shares have traded on the NSE since 27 April 2004 [13].

The FY2015 annual report gives first-production dates. In 1984, Faridabad began production, and in 1991, Barjora Unit I followed. In 2003, Greater Noida and Pithampur started, and in 2008, Ranjangaon followed. Barjora Unit II, the dielectric (capacitor) film line, started in 2014, and was capitalised on 1 March 2015 [11]. The Coex (coextrusion) division grew from Faridabad into Greater Noida and Ranjangaon. The Biax division sits at Barjora in West Bengal. Its core film technology was “originally sourced from U.K.” and the dielectric process was “developed in-house” [14]. The earliest Barjora dates are soft. A secondary source says 1988, the deck 1992 and the annual report 1991 [15][16]. What is firm is the shape of the company. It has three Indian plant locations and a packaging-film heritage that management now disowns (“Xpro is not … a packaging products company”, C. Bhaskar, 22 May 2026). Its dielectric line arrived in 2015 [9].

web_blocks.title: Promoter group and the Birla linkage

web_blocks.html: The promoter is Intellipro Finance Pvt Ltd. The promoter group also includes iPro Capital, Central India General Agents, Birla Holdings, Birla Eastern and Birla family members, led by Chairman Sidharth Birla [12]. At 31 March 2026 the group held 94,61,676 shares, or 40.31% of the company. iPro Capital held 18.79% and Intellipro Finance 14.73% [2]. The company’s website calls the Birla Group an industrial house “headed by a member of the Birla Family” [13]. No filing links Xpro to Hindalco or the Aditya Birla Group; that link was searched for and not found. That this is a separate Birla family branch is our inference, not a company statement.

web_blocks.title: FY2015-FY2018: a new line lands in an oversupplied market

web_blocks.html: The Bruckner dielectric line was the largest investment in the company’s history, funded from internal accruals and a German bank ECB. It arrived when the Indian BOPP market had “significant over-supply resulting in about 70% capacity utilisation and price-based competition” (AR FY2015) [11]. Weak refrigerator demand and OEM down-gauging hit the Coex side at the same time. The Screener series shows operating profit of ₹64 Cr in total over the four years FY2015-FY2018. Interest over the same period was ₹81 Cr, and the cumulative loss was ₹51 Cr (our calculation) [17]. Consolidated borrowings peaked at ₹215 Cr in FY2017 [17].

Operational shocks stacked on the financial ones. Production at Pithampur “has been temporarily suspended since July 2015 following inundation and consequent damage due to heavy rainfall and flash floods” [18]. The unit was sold on 9 June 2018 [19]. The Faridabad Coex unit closed from 23 November 2016. Its land and non-core Kolkata premises were sold in FY2018 for about ₹42 Cr [18][20]. Barjora Unit I, the packaging-grade BOPP line, was restricted from FY2018. It was transferred on 20 October 2022 for ₹6.78 Cr of fixed assets after a 16 April 2019 EGM approval [19][21].

There was no CDR and no BIFR reference. The company rescheduled term loans with its SBI-led consortium and BKB Bank, Germany, effective in the second half of FY2018. The reschedule was “necessitated to overcome the strained cash flow position on account of losses” (AR FY2017) [18]. Promoter-group entities pledged shares in 2019 as extra collateral. The pledges were “finally released” in FY2024 after the banks were repaid [21]. The banks later claimed a ₹2.02 Cr “right to recompense” when loans were prepaid in FY2024 [21]. FY2018’s profit was an asset-sale result. A pre-exceptional loss of ₹11.43 Cr turned into a PAT of ₹10.46 Cr only through ₹21.88 Cr of exceptional income [20].

Debt fell from ₹215 Cr (FY2017) to ₹39 Cr (FY2023), an 81.9% reduction (our calculation) [17]. The company reports debt cuts of ₹45.87 Cr in FY2022 and ₹63.97 Cr in FY2023, and says “all normal long term loans” were repaid “well before schedule” [22][23]. A six-month Covid moratorium was taken, but management withdrew its restructuring proposal because cash flow met repayments [24]. Ind-Ra put FY2022 EBITDA at ₹63.8 Cr, a 13.5% margin against 11% in FY2021 and 8.6% in FY2020. It put net leverage at 1.08x versus 3.2x in FY2021 and 5.3x in FY2020 [25].

web_blocks.caption: The turnaround was price and mix, not tonnes; Biax and Coex net sales, ₹ Cr
web_blocks.takeaway: Biax sales rose 113.4% on 10.6% more tonnes (our calculation from annual-report divisional figures). The dielectric line’s recovery therefore came overwhelmingly from realisation and mix [20][19][26][24][22][23].

web_blocks.html: Ind-Ra’s rating path tracked the recovery. On 17 November 2021, Ind-Ra rated it BBB/Positive, and on 10 August 2022, it moved to BBB+ [27][25]. On 28 August 2023, it moved to A-, and on 15 October 2024, it upgraded the short-term rating to A1 [28][29]. It affirmed A-/Stable/A1 with ₹195 Cr of facilities on 14 January 2026 [30]. The standalone company says it has been “continuously profitable since 2017-18” [2].

web_blocks.title: The revenue, margin and profit cycle, FY2015-FY2026

web_blocks.caption: Consolidated cycle table, ₹ Cr; Screener-derived, operating profit after FX differences, borrowings include leases from FY2025
rows: Dielectric line capitalised into BOPP oversupply
web_blocks.takeaway: Revenue compounded 8.8% a year FY2015-FY2023 and then fell 0.8% FY2023-FY2026, while operating profit fell 56.8%. PAT fell 55.6% (our calculation) [17]. The company’s own FY2026 EBITDA before FX was ₹47.4 Cr [2].

web_blocks.html: Three preferential or QIP raises brought in ₹439.95 Cr of equity at parent level (our calculation). The first was 19,68,000 warrants at ₹762 in January 2022 (₹149.96 Cr). Malabar India Fund took 16,40,000 of them and two promoter-group entities 3,28,000 [22]. The second was 14,35,750 warrants at ₹975 in January 2024 (₹139.99 Cr, 12 subscribers) [21]. The third was a QIP of 13,62,397 shares at ₹1,101 on 29 February 2024 (₹150 Cr gross, 21 subscribers) [12][31]. A 1-for-2 bonus issue of 59,06,744 shares was allotted on 6 July 2022 [23].

web_blocks.caption: Equity share count (₹10 face value)
web_blocks.takeaway: The count rose 98.7% from FY2022 to FY2026, or 32.4% after stripping out the bonus (our calculation). The ₹439.95 Cr raised ahead of a ₹700+ Cr programme is what the rest of this chapter is about [23][22][21][2].

web_blocks.html: Promoter holding moved from about 50.0% (FY2016-FY2022) to 51.4% (March 2023, promoter warrant exercise). It then fell to 45.3% (December 2023), 42.5% (March 2024), 42.4% (March 2025) and 40.3% since September 2025 [32]. In absolute shares the promoters did not sell. They held 93,55,926 at 30 September 2024 and 94,61,676 at 30 September 2026, the difference being their 1,05,750 warrant shares. So the fall is dilution by allotments to others [33][34]. Malabar India Fund holds 26,60,000 shares, or 11.33% [2]. We reconcile that holding as 24,60,000 shares from the 2022 warrants including bonus plus 2,00,000 from 2024 (our calculation). The FY2024 annual report told shareholders these issues “marked the end of our foreseeable capital-raising actions” [21]. The next equity was a 15% sale of the UAE subsidiary to Oasis II Investments Holdings (AED 33.09 mn) on 12 December 2025 [2].

web_blocks.title: 2024-2026: the capex pivot and the slipped timelines

web_blocks.html: The programme has three stages. Barjora Line 2 doubles Indian dielectric nameplate from 4,000 to 8,000 MT. It was estimated at ₹284.61 Cr in the Placement Document, of which ₹145.99 Cr was the core line ordered from a European supplier on 7 December 2022 [12]. It was capitalised at ₹212.34 Cr on 27 March 2026, which is 74.6% of the estimate (our calculation) [2]. Management verbally said about ₹240 Cr [9]. The UAE line, in subsidiary Xpro Dielectric Films FZ-LLC at Ras Al Khaimah, was announced at 4,500 TPA and “over AED 100 million” [35]. Consolidated capital work-in-progress was ₹299.5 Cr at 31 March 2026 [14] and ₹360.0 Cr at 30 September 2026 [36]. That is roughly AED 140 mn at current rates (our calculation). Lines 4 and 5 are only “on the roadmap” [2].

web_blocks.takeaway: Barjora Line 2 arrived about 15 months after the Q3 FY2025 commitment. The UAE line is at least 18 months behind its Q2 2025 date even if it meets March 2027 (our calculation, dates per [37][38][35][39][1][9][3]).

web_blocks.html: The AR FY2026 Directors’ Report said “the earlier delays in the project were externally driven and are behind us” on 20 May 2026 [2]; the UAE schedule then slipped past its August-September trial date [3].

web_blocks.title: The share-price cycle (added after the price-blind pass)

web_blocks.html: Chapters 1 to 6 were written without sight of the share price. That let the business be judged before the market's opinion of it was known. With that work locked, the price history can now be laid over the operating history. All prices are closing prices adjusted for the 2022 bonus, from dated Yahoo Finance bars to the 12 November 2026 session [40]. From its NSE listing in April 2004 until early 2021, Xpro never closed above ₹55.2. It fell to ₹8.5 at the Covid low on 23 March 2020 (our calculation from the series). Then the dielectric earnings turn arrived. The stock went from ₹48.7 on 31 March 2021 to a closing high of ₹1,075.8 on 24 March 2022, a 22.1x move in twelve months [40]. Over the same period PAT rose from ₹8 Cr to ₹45 Cr [32].

web_blocks.caption: Share-price cycle by fiscal year (closing prices, adjusted for the 2022 bonus issue)
rows: A sub-₹60 stock for 17 years; the Covid low came after three near-zero profit years
Dielectric earnings turn; a 22.1x move from the 31 Mar 2021 close to the March 2022 high
Peak-to-trough fall of 49.9% from the March 2022 high while profit held at ₹45 Cr
Capacity story and the ₹150 Cr QIP at ₹1,101 priced in February 2024
All-time closing high while FY2025 PAT fell to ₹38 Cr
Peak-to-trough fall of 50.3% from the December 2024 high; Barjora Line 2 slips to March 2026
Rebound, 35.9% pullback, then a 14.6% bounce after the Q2 results
web_blocks.takeaway: Two peak-to-trough falls of about 50% in four years (FY2023 and FY2026) sit inside a 23.5x gain since March 2021. The multiple, not earnings, did most of the work in the last three years [40].

web_blocks.html: The capital-raising prices fit this map. The January 2022 warrants at ₹762 were struck before the 1:2 bonus. That equals ₹508 on the bonus-adjusted series used here [22]. The February 2024 QIP at ₹1,101 was 2.17x that adjusted price [12]. Management raised equity into strength twice and then told shareholders the programme was complete. That is why the 40.3% promoter holding reflects dilution and not selling (see above) [21].

The second leg is the one that matters for today. From the closing high of ₹1,634.4 on 17 December 2024 the stock fell 50.3% in 309 trading sessions to ₹813.0 on 13 March 2026. In that period Barjora Line 2 slipped from the promised second half of FY2025 to March 2026, and EPS fell from ₹17.04 to ₹8.19 [41][1][40]. The stock then rebounded 84.9% to ₹1,503.6 on 2 July 2026 and gave back 35.9% to ₹963.6 on 2 November. It rose 14.6% between 3 and 12 November as the Q2 FY2027 results showed revenue up 47% [3][40]. Our reading is that this stock trades on the capacity narrative and reprices by half whenever a date slips. The narrative must therefore be tested against valuation (Chapter 7) and the chart (Chapter 8) before any capital is committed.

web_blocks.takeaway: Every capital event after 2021 is tied to one purpose, doubling and then tripling dielectric capacity.

web_blocks.html: Evidence of resilience. The company absorbed four years of thin or negative earnings, a flood and a plant closure without CDR or BIFR. It then repaid its banks early, released the promoter pledges, lifted its rating from BBB to A-, and has kept a clean audit record [18][21][23][8]. The promoters did not sell shares. If history is a guide, the balance sheet can absorb a delayed ramp. Net debt is only about ₹40 Cr against equity of ₹813 Cr at 30 September 2026 (our calculation) [36].

The warning pattern. Each of the last two capex cycles has been followed by margin compression and slipped dates. The 2015 line landed in oversupply and produced cumulative losses. In the 2024-26 programme, consolidated operating margin fell from 14.5% (FY2023) to 6.3% (FY2026) while volumes were flat [17][9]. Prices were also cut 6-7% “in anticipation of the creation of new capacities” [41]. Timelines slipped by 15 months on Line 2 and at least 18 on the UAE line, and the UAE cost has run above the 2024 headline. Our judgment is that Xpro is a proven survivor and a weak estimator of commissioning dates. We would haircut any management schedule by about a year. We would judge the programme on whether Line 2 reaches the 70-80% utilisation it guided for Q4 FY2027, not on announcements.

book_paragraphs: Let me start with a question you should ask about every company you study: what has it already survived? Xpro India was born on paper in November 1997 as Biax Films and renamed itself Xpro in September 1998. Its plants arrived through a court-sanctioned demerger from a Birla group company called Cimmco Birla, approved by the High Courts of Calcutta and Madhya Pradesh in 1999 [12]. It has traded on the National Stock Exchange since April 2004 [13]. Notice how ordinary that sounds. Nothing in this origin story hints at a capacitor-film specialist.

The plants came first. Faridabad opened in 1984, Barjora in 1991, Greater Noida and Pithampur in 2003 and Ranjangaon in 2008 [11]. Two industrial processes sit under the Xpro name. One is BOPP, short for biaxially oriented polypropylene: you melt plastic, then stretch the film in both directions until it is thin, strong and flat, and at Barjora the technology was originally sourced from the United Kingdom and later developed in house [14]. The other is coextrusion, which melts several plastics together into one layered sheet. Management is blunt about what this is not. As C. Bhaskar put it on 22 May 2026, “Xpro is not - I would like to emphasize on the NOT, a packaging products company as we are often considered to be” [9].

You will hear the Birla name and wonder whether this is the same family as Hindalco and the Aditya Birla Group. I looked, and I could not find that link in any filing. The promoter is Intellipro Finance, joined by iPro Capital, Birla Holdings, Birla Eastern and family members led by Chairman Sidharth Birla, and together they hold about 40% [12][2]. That this is a different branch of the family is my inference, not something the company says. When a record is silent, I say so rather than fill in the gap.

Now picture 2015. Barjora’s second line, the one that makes dielectric film, the thin polypropylene film that goes inside capacitors, has just been switched on. It is the biggest investment the company has ever made, and the directors write down their own warning: it was to be expected that interest and depreciation burdens would exert significant pressure on the bottom line [11]. Around them the general packaging-film market was in oversupply, running at about 70% of capacity [11]. Then, in July 2015, production at Pithampur “has been temporarily suspended … following inundation and consequent damage due to heavy rainfall and flash floods” [18]. In November 2016 the Faridabad plant closed [18].

Here is the arithmetic that tells the story. Over four years the business earned ₹64 Cr of operating profit and paid ₹81 Cr of interest, a cumulative loss of ₹51 Cr [17]. Debt peaked at ₹215 Cr [17]. A company in that spot often ends up in a formal restructuring, called CDR, where lenders take losses and the process is public. Xpro instead rescheduled its loans with its State Bank of India-led lenders and a German bank, a rescheduling that the annual report says was “necessitated to overcome the strained cash flow position on account of losses” [18]. It sold land and units to pay down debt. Even FY2018’s reported profit of ₹10.46 Cr came from ₹21.88 Cr of asset-sale gains [20]. You and I should not call that a recovery. Promoter-group entities also pledged shares in 2019 as extra comfort for the banks, and those pledges were released only in FY2024 [21].

Think about what clearing the decks looked like in practice. The Pithampur unit was sold on 9 June 2018 [19]. Faridabad’s land and some non-core Kolkata property went for about ₹42 Cr in FY2018 [20]. Barjora’s older packaging-grade line, Unit I, was restricted from FY2018, approved for sale at a shareholders’ meeting on 16 April 2019 and finally handed over on 20 October 2022 for ₹6.78 Cr of fixed assets [19][21]. Each of those decisions shrank the company, and each moved it away from commodity packaging film toward dielectric film and coextruded sheet. That is the quiet strategic result of the loss years: the portfolio you see today was shaped by the plants that had to go.

The real recovery came after 2019, and how it happened matters. Between FY2018 and FY2023 dielectric sales more than doubled, but tonnage rose only about 11% [20][23]. In plain English, the company did not sell much more film; it sold better film at higher prices, roughly ₹228 a kilogram rising to ₹439 by my arithmetic [20][23]. Covid brought a six-month loan moratorium, but management withdrew its restructuring proposal when cash flow proved enough [24]. By FY2022 the rating agency saw EBITDA of ₹63.8 Cr at a 13.5% margin, and net leverage had fallen from 5.3 times to 1.08 times in two years [25]. By FY2023 debt was ₹39 Cr, and the company said “all normal long term loans” were repaid “well before schedule” [23]. The agency lifted the company from BBB to A- over 2021 to 2023 [27][25][28]. That is real evidence of resilience, and I do not want you to underrate it.

Put the whole cycle on one line. Revenue compounded about 8.8% a year from FY2015 to FY2023 and has been flat since. Operating margin climbed from about 1% to a peak of 14.5% in FY2023 and then dropped to 6.3% in FY2026, while profit after tax fell by more than half from its FY2023 level [17]. The company’s own EBITDA, before currency effects, was ₹47.4 Cr in FY2026 [2]. A business that was shrinking its debt a few years ago now reports a lower profit on a much bigger balance sheet. Keep that gap in mind; the rest of the book explains it.

Next, the capital. Between January 2022 and February 2024 the company raised ₹439.95 Cr from shareholders in three steps [22][21][12]. Two were rounds of warrants, which are options an investor pays part of the price for upfront and converts into shares later, at ₹762 in 2022 and ₹975 in 2024. The third was a qualified institutional placement, or QIP, a quick route to sell shares to large institutions, at ₹1,101 for ₹150 Cr [12]. A bonus issue of one new share for every two held was added in July 2022 [23]. The result is that shares outstanding went from about 1.18 crore to 2.35 crore, a rise of about a third once the bonus is set aside [2]. The promoters did not sell; their percentage fell from 51.4% to 40.3% because new shares went to other people [32][33]. Malabar India Fund, a foreign portfolio investor, is the largest outside holder at 11.33% [2].

It helps to know who bought. In the 2022 warrant round, Malabar India Fund took 16,40,000 of the 19,68,000 warrants and two promoter-group entities took the other 3,28,000 [22][31]. The 2024 warrants went to 12 subscribers, including more Malabar entities and the two promoter-group entities, and the QIP went to 21 institutions [21][12]. I am describing a capital transaction here, nothing more: these were the people the company chose to sell new shares to, at the prices the company set.

The annual report for FY2024 told shareholders these issues “marked the end of our foreseeable capital-raising actions” [21]. Keep that sentence in mind, because in December 2025 the UAE subsidiary sold 15% of itself to an Abu Dhabi investor [2]. The parent kept its word; its subsidiary simply did not need to.

Now to the pivot. The money was meant to build new dielectric lines. Barjora’s second line doubled Indian capacity from 4,000 to 8,000 tonnes a year and was capitalised at ₹212.34 Cr, about three-quarters of the ₹284.61 Cr estimated in the placement document [12][2]. A third line is going up at Ras Al Khaimah in the UAE, announced at “over AED 100 million” and carried at ₹360 Cr of work-in-progress by September 2026, which is roughly AED 140 million by my arithmetic [35][14][36]. Work-in-progress, or CWIP, is simply money spent on a plant that is not yet producing, and it earns nothing until it is switched on.

Then look at the dates. On 29 May 2024 management said, “We should be operational definitely in the third quarter of the current fiscal” [38]. Commercial production was declared on 27 March 2026, about fifteen months later [2]. The board wrote in the FY2026 annual report that “the earlier delays in the project were externally driven and are behind us” [2]. The UAE line has since slipped past its August-September 2026 trial date, and it is already at least eighteen months behind its first public date [3][35]. Earlier, in November 2025, the company had written that “the Board and management understand and share shareholders’ disappointment during this trying phase” [1].

The slippage did not arrive in one blow. In May 2023 management expected the first new line to contribute in FY2025 and the second in FY2026 [37]. In May 2024 that became the third quarter of FY2025. In May 2025 an analyst asked whether commercial production would start by September and the answer was that this was “a reasonable assumption” [39]. By November 2025 the company said the formal start-up had taken longer than planned because of external factors [1]. Each date was missed by a few months, and the misses added up to more than a year. That pattern, not any single delay, is what I would ask you to remember.

One more fact balances the picture. India Ratings affirmed the company at A- with a stable outlook and a short-term grade of A1 on 14 January 2026, and it assigned ₹195 Cr of bank facilities in total [30]. The company also says it has been “continuously profitable since 2017-18” [2]. A rating agency looks at the same history you and I are reading, and it did not downgrade after the delays. That is not a guarantee of anything, but it is evidence that lenders still see the balance sheet as sound.

Now that the business history is done, let me show you the other half of the story, the price, which I deliberately kept out of the earlier chapters so that nothing about the market's mood could colour our reading of the company. Between its listing in 2004 and the spring of 2021, Xpro's stock never closed above ₹55.2 on the adjusted series, and on 23 March 2020 it touched ₹8.5. Then the dielectric earnings arrived, and in twelve months the price went from ₹48.7 to ₹1,075.8, a 22.1 times move [40]. Ask yourself what it felt like to hold it through the next four years. Twice the stock lost about half its value from a peak: 49.9% between March 2022 and February 2023, and 50.3% between December 2024 and March 2026 [40]. The second fall happened while Barjora's second line kept missing its start-up date, and EPS dropped from ₹17.04 to ₹8.19. The price had been paying for the ramp, and each slipped date made the market pay a little less for it. Since March 2023 the shares are up 65% even though earnings per share are down 67%, which tells you the market is buying the future and not the present. Hold that thought; Chapter 7 puts a number on how much of the future the price already contains.

Let me give you a way to hold both sides in your head. The bull reading is that this company has already survived worse. Its balance sheet carries net debt of only about ₹40 Cr against equity of ₹813 Cr, so a slow ramp is survivable [36]. The skeptic’s reading is that it has now built into a headwind twice. After the 2015 line came oversupply and losses; after the 2024-26 build came a fall in operating margin from 14.5% to 6.3% while volumes stood still and prices were cut 6-7% [17][41]. Charlie Munger said, “Show me the incentive and I’ll show you the outcome,” and the incentive here is capacity, because a larger plant is the only way this business grows.

My own judgment, in one sentence: Xpro is a proven survivor and a poor forecaster of its own start-up dates. I would haircut management’s schedules by about a year, and I would judge the programme on whether Line 2 reaches the 70-80% utilisation guided for the quarter ending March 2027, not on announcements [3]. The share-price cycle continues into valuation and tape in Chapters 7 and 8.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: This company has already passed one hard test: it lost money for years, never restructured formally, and repaid its banks early. The second test is different. It is not survival but whether new capacity earns more than it costs. The history says Xpro will probably survive the answer; it does not yet say the answer is good.
